newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss see international WWII conference this year.
newsitem.headline: Swiss see international WWII conference this year.

text.p: The chairman of a Swiss historical commission probing Switzerland's controversial role as a World War Two financial centre expects an international conference on the Nazi era to convene later this year, he told a newspaper.

Jean-Francois Bergier, head of the nine-member panel, told the Blick daily in an interview published on Wednesday that bringing togther experts investigating the era could curb duplication of effort and coordinate the flow of information.

U.S. Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, who helped compile a 200-page report on Nazi gold deals with Switzerland and other countries, has proposed holding an international conference this year on the flow of Nazi assets after the war.
Bergier said he had first raised the idea with Eizenstat.
"Stuart Eizenstat and I had discussed this already in February," Bergier said. "I have already established initial contact with other countries' historians commissions."
Asked when such a conference could he held, he said: "I think in early autumn."

The U.S. study, made public last week, criticised Switzerland for banking Nazi gold during and after World War Two and gave evidence that some gold the Nazis sold to the Swiss was taken from Holocaust victims.

The seven-month study said the Reichsbank had an account for melted-down loot from death camp victims, such as rings, coins and gold teeth, and sold some of this along with gold taken from occupied countries to finance the German war machine.

Swiss officials cautiously welcomed the report but said it failed to appreciate properly the fact that their tiny, neutral country was surrounded by the Axis powers for most of the war and depended on trade with them for its survival.
The report said there was no evidence Swiss officials knew at the time that gold bought from the Nazis might include gold stolen from individual Holocaust victims.
Bergier, whose nine-member panel can penetrate Swiss banking secrecy surrounding wartime events, said the Eizenstat report held nothing new for him.
"It is valuable for making some things more precise. But to me the information about so-called victims' gold is just hypothesis for the time being," he said.
